tier_reason: Upgraded from D: the original benchmark_url (README FAQ 'How fast is it?') has only a qualitative Python comparison, but an independent third-party repo (MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame, benchmark_runs/bench_pylua.csv, summary.ipynb, runner runbench.janet, bench_pylua.jdn) times Janet against CPython on seven Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs with CPU model (i5-7500) and Janet CFLAGS stated. Not A: the C compiler is not named and the Python baseline is an Anaconda 3.8 binary with no build details; it is a small personal repo, single run, not a well-known suite, so the orchestrator may prefer to cap it at C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Mixed, not an across-the-board win. README FAQ (qualitative only): programs 'tend to be a bit faster than they would be in a language like Python', VM 'about the same speed as most interpreted languages without a JIT compiler', 'YMMV'. Independent run (MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame, Janet 1.14.1 vs Python 3.8, user+sys seconds): Janet faster on binarytrees 71.63 vs 110.94 s (1.55x), knucleotide 137.59 vs 164.44 s (1.20x), nbody 17.53 vs 37.77 s (2.15x); slower on fannkuch 5.04 vs 4.83 s, reverse-complement 35.78 vs 7.37 s (4.9x slower), pidigits 5.98 vs 3.92 s, regexredux 15.86 vs 13.51 s. Geometric mean over the seven: Janet about 1.12x slower than CPython (derived from page data). Lua 5.4 beat Janet on fannkuch, knucleotide, nbody and reverse-complement.
corrections.workload: Computer Language Benchmarks Game programs, single-threaded idiomatic versions: fannkuch n=10, binarytrees depth 21, knucleotide on a 25M-line input, nbody 5,000,000 steps, reverse-complement on a 100M input, pidigits 10000 digits (Python uses built-in big ints), regexredux on a 5M input. Timed by runbench.janet as user+system CPU seconds from /usr/bin/time, one run each; only the exit code is checked, not the output.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Janet 1.14.1 built with CFLAGS='-fPIC -O2 -flto' (C compiler not named); Python 3.8 from Anaconda (prebuilt binary); Lua 5.4.
corrections.hardware: Intel Core i5-7500 @ 3.40GHz, 4 cores, hyperthreading disabled
corrections.caveats: No first-party numbers: the README FAQ's 'a bit faster than Python' is hedged and qualitative, and the same FAQ says tight critical loops should be written in C or C++. The only Janet-versus-CPython timings found are a small independent repo (16 stars, last commit 2022-04-04, no license file) from 2021 on Janet 1.14.1 and Python 3.8: Janet won 3 of 7 benchmarks (pure-interpreter object and float work: binarytrees, nbody, knucleotide) and lost 4 where Python's C-implemented builtins do the work (bytes.translate, re, big ints), for a geometric mean about 1.12x slower (derived from page data). Versions are dated: CPython 3.11+ is substantially faster than 3.8 and Janet has had many releases since, so current standing is unmeasured. Single run per benchmark, no output validation.

notes: Metadata checked on github.com: MIT, 4.4k stars, 281 forks, not archived, last commit 2026-10-06 (active). Record's README paraphrase is accurate; I added the independent MikeBeller/janet-benchmarksgame numbers, which show Janet is not faster than CPython overall (faster on binarytrees 1.55x, knucleotide 1.20x, nbody 2.15x; slower on fannkuch, reverse-complement 4.9x, pidigits, regexredux; geomean about 1.12x slower). Shortcomings to record: claim only holds for interpreter-bound workloads, evidence dated (Janet 1.14.1, Python 3.8), compiler unnamed, single run; GitHub discussion #1239 has only anecdote ('faster than Python, but not quite as fast as PyPy').
